7.0.s.en: (1) Elisha's prophecy of the end of the famine

7.0.0.en: Shekel: a shekel of gold, equal to about 11.3-11.6 grams.

7.0.1.en: After the king declared his helplessness and expected evil, namely the surrender of the city and death for himself and his men, God intervened through the mouth of His prophet Elisha to announce a solution that no one had expected. Elisha prophesied, in front of the king and his messenger, in front of the elders who were gathered with him, and in front of all the sons of the prophets who served with him, with the word of the Lord, that about this time tomorrow flour and barley would be available in abundance, so that their prices would fall enormously, and a measure of fine flour would be sold for a shekel, and likewise two measures of barley for a shekel, in the market of Samaria.

7.1.0.en: Windows: the plural of a window (kuwwa), meaning an opening.

7.1.1.en: The king and all who were present heard Elisha's words and marveled. Some believed, and some were troubled by a measure of doubt. But the king's own officer, who was the king's bodyguard and adviser and on whom the king leaned as he walked, when he heard Elisha's prophecy about the end of the famine, scoffed at the prophet's words and said mockingly, "Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?" Elisha answered him that he would see it happen but, as a punishment for his mockery, would not eat of it, that is, of the flour and barley that would be found in abundance. The king did not believe Elisha's prophecy, as is clear from (v. 12), but he kept silent; this officer, however, mocked the word of God, and so he deserved the divine punishment, namely death.

7.1.2.en: Elisha's words were illogical, for if good came upon the whole city, the first to receive of it would be the king, then his aide and personal guard on whom he leaned. But God's judgments surpass all reason, and He punishes the scoffers and blesses His humble children.

7.1.3.en: The Lord is very long-suffering toward sinners, but there is no salvation for those who scoff at His word. They exist today as they have in every age; they show unbelief and argue, and the word of God is vain in their eyes. Their destruction is certain. May you reject the thoughts of doubt that Satan casts into your mind against the promises of God, or the sacraments of the Church, or any spiritual blessings you can receive from the holy children of God, so that you do not lose the many graces that God wants to give you.

7.2.s.en: (2) The lifting of the siege and the flight of the Arameans

7.2.0.en: There were four leprous men at the entrance of the city gate, talking together, and one of them urged them to take a positive step that would settle the matter, instead of resigning themselves to death by hunger.

7.2.1.en: These lepers were outcasts; because of their uncleanness they lived outside the camp, that is, outside the city, so that no one would become unclean by touching them. The people of the city used to throw them some food. When the famine became severe, no one threw them any food at all, and they were close to dying of hunger. So they began to think positively about a solution to the problem for themselves, and after that for the rest of the city, as we shall see in the following verses. God uses these lepers to solve the problem of the city, as we shall see.

7.2.2.en: Do not despise any person, however lowly he may seem, or weak, or rejected by people, for he is the image of God, and God is able to work through him and in him, giving you good by his means, and you may learn many things from him.

7.2.3.en: The severe distress that these four lepers suffered, being kept away from other people and exposed to death by hunger, made them look for a solution. A severe crisis that brings a person close to death makes him think of a positive solution. So do not be alarmed if the affliction increases and becomes unbearable, for this may be the beginning of the solution of the problem.

7.3.0.en: The four lepers began to talk together and said that if we try to enter the city of Samaria and break the law that requires us to stay away from the cities because of our leprosy, we will find no food and will die of hunger; and if we stay where we are outside the city, we will also die of hunger. One of them made a suggestion: that they go over to the Arameans and surrender to them. If the Arameans accepted them, they would save their lives, live and find food; and if they killed them as enemies, so be it, since death would overtake them by any means. In this way God put this courage in them, so that they might save themselves and also their city. They did not give in to death and despair but moved, hoping to find life. Jewish tradition says that the four lepers were Gehazi and his sons; and since Gehazi knew God, perhaps he prayed and God guided him to this idea, so that he might save himself and his city.

7.4.0.en: Twilight: that is, the evening, the time of sunset just before darkness.

7.4.1.en: The uttermost part of the camp of the Arameans: the farthest end of the Aramean camp, the part toward the city of Samaria.

7.4.2.en: The rest of the lepers approved their companion's suggestion, agreed to it and decided to carry it out. When evening came they arose and went to the camp of the Arameans, but they found not a single soldier there; the camp was completely empty of Arameans.

7.5.0.en: The Holy Bible explains why the Aramean camp was empty of all the soldiers: they had heard the noise of chariots and horses, that is, the noise of a great army advancing against them. The noise was powerful because it was from God. So they thought that the king of Israel had hired against them the kings of the Hittites, who lived in the north of the Levant, that is, present-day Syria, and the kings of the Egyptians, for Egypt was at that time divided into more than one part, each part having a king. What the Arameans thought was illogical, for how could the king of Israel hire against them strong armies like these while he was besieged inside his city? But just as God had closed their eyes with blindness before Elisha, now He closes their minds, so that they imagine strange, frightening things and flee quickly, leaving all their possessions behind them.

7.6.0.en: This conclusion terrified the soldiers of the Aramean army, for they imagined that they were certainly defeated. So they left their camp, their horses and their donkeys as they were, and fled to save their lives.

7.7.0.en: When the four lepers found the camp quiet, with no one in it, they took courage and entered one of the tents at the edge of the camp. They found much food in it, and they ate and drank; then they took the silver, the clothing and everything of value that was in it, and went out, and dug a hole and hid the spoil in it. Then they returned to the Aramean camp and entered a second tent, took what was in it, went away, dug in the ground and hid what they had taken. And when they felt that they stood before a great treasure, they took from it as much as they were able to carry.

7.8.0.en: After taking spoil from the two tents, the four lepers realized that before them was a camp full of tents, with much spoil inside them and around them. So they came to themselves and said that it was not right to delay bringing the good news to our brethren in Samaria, so that they too might come and eat and take much spoil. They decided to hurry to tell the king during the night, so that no harm would come to them, for if morning came the king might be angry with them for their delay in telling him. All the more would God be angry with them for neglecting to bring the good news to their brethren and sinking into selfishness, so that they did not feel their brethren's hunger. It is a beautiful thing that they hurried to tell the guards standing before the king's house; for delaying to bring good news to others and to make them glad is a grave matter that angers God.

7.8.1.en: And if these lepers were Gehazi and his sons, then Gehazi moved from the greed and selfishness that marked him in the story of Naaman, when he took gifts, to sensitivity toward others, feeling their needs and caring that they should share in God's grace and blessings, so that they might come out of hunger and be satisfied, and even enjoy abundance.

7.8.2.en: Take care to look after those around you spiritually and to encourage them to attach themselves to the Church, so that they may taste the sweetness of fellowship with God and you may win them for Christ. And be careful to taste first, yourself, fellowship with God in the Church, through the sacraments and the means of grace, so that when you have experienced the power of God within you, you may move with zeal to call others to be joined to God. So it was with the lepers: they ate and were satisfied, and their hearts were moved with love toward their brethren, and they hurried to bring them the good news, so that they too might go out and eat and take spoil.

7.9.0.en: The four lepers came to the gate of the city of Samaria but did not enter, because entry was forbidden to them on account of their leprosy. So they called to the porter of the city, who, when he heard their shouting, opened the gate and came out to them. They told him that they had entered the camp of the Arameans and had found no one there, not a single soldier, but had found horses and donkeys tied and tents still standing with all their contents.

7.10.0.en: The porter of the city told his fellow porters at the city gate, and sent word to the porters of the king's house during the night, charging them to tell the king. So they spoke to those in charge inside the house and informed the king of what had happened.

7.11.0.en: When the king heard, he did not believe that the power of God had driven out the Arameans so that they left their possessions and fled, and that thereby the prophecy of the prophet Elisha was being fulfilled. Instead, with his reason, he doubted what had happened and thought it a trick of the Arameans, who had left their tents and hidden in one of the fields to ambush the people of Samaria, so that if they came out to take the spoil, the Arameans would fall upon them and kill them, then storm the city and occupy it. This doubting speech, if we examine it closely, is not logical. For although ambush in war was common and well known in those times, there are things that prevent this supposition, namely:

7.11.1.en: 1- The people of Samaria were in great fear, so how would they dare to send spies to the camp of the Arameans? Of course they would not go out, lest they die.

7.11.2.en: 2- The people of Samaria were in severe hunger and were almost surrendering, as the king showed in (ch. 25, 33); so the Arameans had no need to devise new plans to bring the city down.

7.11.3.en: Using your reason more than is proper makes you fall into distress, so that you refuse to believe the promises of God, because His promises surpass reason. So obey God's commandments, trusting in His power that supports you, that you may enjoy inexpressible blessings.

7.12.0.en: When one of the king's servants and advisers saw the king's doubt, he offered a suggestion to make sure whether or not there was an ambush. He said: let us look for five horses that may have remained in the city, since the rest of the horses have died of hunger, or have become weak and unable to walk, or have been eaten by the people of the city; let us send them with their chariots and soldiers to the camp of the Arameans, that they may make sure that no one is in the camp and that there is no ambush. If they live and return to us, they are like all the multitude of the living in the city, and they will bring joyful news, and these living ones will live by the spoil they take. But if the Arameans rise against them and kill them, they will be like the multitude of people and horses that have died. That is, his suggestion was to send spies, or emissaries, to make sure there was no ambush.

7.13.1.en: Indeed, two chariots with horses were prepared, and they set out with the soldiers in them until they reached the camp of the Arameans, which was empty of soldiers. Then they continued on, searching for the Arameans, until they reached the river Jordan. They noticed that the road was full of garments and vessels that the Arameans had thrown away in their flight, out of their fear and panic, as their aim was to cross the river Jordan and hurry back to their own country. The distance between Samaria and the river Jordan is great, and this shows the extent of the Arameans' terror, which lasted a long time, until they returned to their country. Most likely God made them hear the sound of armies pursuing them, so that they fled and returned to their country. And the messengers told the king all that they had seen.

7.14.0.en: The hungry people went out and plundered the contents of the Aramean camp; they ate and were satisfied and possessed much spoil. In this the prophecy of Elisha was fulfilled, for a measure of fine flour became a shekel and two measures of barley a shekel, exactly as the Lord had spoken through the mouth of His prophet.

7.15.s.en: (3) The death of the scoffing officer

7.15.0.en: The king made sure that the Aramean camp was empty of soldiers and that there was spoil and much food, and the news spread through the city. There was great joy among all the people, who had almost died of hunger, and they grew strong and hurried to plunder food, to eat and to live. The king hurried to organize the movement out of the city, lest the people trample one another in their eagerness for food in order to live. He sent his personal guard, that is, the officer on whom he used to lean when he walked, and most likely a group of soldiers was with him, to organize the going out of the people. This guard rejoiced, and at the same time was ashamed because of his mockery of the word of God, spoken through the mouth of His prophet Elisha, when he stood with the king at the door of the prophet's house. The guard tried to organize the going out as much as he could, but the rush of the hungry people was greater than any imagining, so that they threw this guard to the ground and trampled him under their feet, and he died, and perhaps others of the people also fell and died. Thus Elisha's word was fulfilled, that this officer would see the fulfillment of the word of God in the abundance of food but would not eat of it, because he would be dead.

7.15.1.en: Do not challenge God and reject His word. Even if doubts war against you, resist them, for who are you that you should rebel against God? The mercy of God comes upon the weak, but it rejects the scoffers and the rebellious, who receive nothing but divine wrath.

7.15.2.en: The return of the Shunammite, and the reigns of Hazael, Jehoram and Ahaziah. (1) The Shunammite recovers her land (vv. 1-6)

7.15.3.en: 1- Then spake Elisha unto the woman, whose son he had restored to life, saying, Arise, and go thou and thine household, and sojourn wheresoever thou canst sojourn: for the LORD hath called for a famine; and it shall also come upon the land seven years. 2- And the woman arose, and did after the saying of the man of God: and she went with her household, and sojourned in the land of the Philistines seven years. 3- And it came to pass at the seven years' end, that the woman returned out of the land of the Philistines: and she went forth to cry unto the king for her house and for her land. 4- And the king talked with Gehazi the servant of the man of God, saying, Tell me, I pray thee, all the great things that Elisha hath done. 5- And it came to pass, as he was telling the king how he had restored a dead body to life, that, behold, the woman, whose son he had restored to life, cried to the king for her house and for her land. And Gehazi said, My lord, O king, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha restored to life. 6- And when the king asked the woman, she told him. So the king appointed unto her a certain officer, saying, Restore all that was hers, and all the fruits of the field since the day that she left the land, even until now.
